## 7. Hostile validation (HV) and review

Review and hostile-validation (HV) guidance (operator-directed, 2026-10-09). Applies to every agent, plan, and review loop.

### 7.1 Adversarial review of tracked results (locked 2026-08-12)

1. Validate independently through a hostile reviewer wherever the plan calls for HV and before any done state (section 4.5). Self-check alone is not validation.
2. Every result is timestamped with a sortable local date and time (section 3.1).
3. Every FAIL and UNKNOWN from the review is shown to the operator.
4. Every result includes an accuracy rating and a completeness rating.

Reviewer (resolution of 2026-10-13, verbatim): "HV must not be executed by the same agent family as the requesting agent.  If not specified by operator, ask what agent and model to use for HV in a session." HV uses the reviewer and tooling explicitly authorized for the session. Verify the reviewer's model and effort from its own runtime receipts.

Review time is unbounded (operator, 2026-10-12, verbatim: "Do not bound review time"): no timeout, kill, deadline, or wait limit on any HV reviewer run, and no expected duration in briefs or plans; the implementer only checks the response stream in repeated read-only waits until the run completes, however long the review takes.

HV is not bounded by size either, and a stall is the one reason to end a reviewer (added 2026-10-28; operator, 2026-10-28T21:57:09, verbatim: "HV invocations should not be bounded by time or size.  Only if it stops updating for longet than 30 minutes should you kill it."): no cap on the evidence a request supplies or on what the reviewer reads or writes (briefs carry no file-size limit); end the reviewer only when its response stream has had no update for more than 30 minutes, record that run as stopped, not evidence, and relaunch. Committing a receipt GitHub refuses as a compressed copy, with the original kept, is not a bound on the review.

When HV runs (resolution of 2026-10-13, verbatim): "HV cadence is an artifact of the plan, not a standing rule." Section 4.5 still requires hostile AGREE before any done state.

HV at a phase exit (approved 2026-11-03): when the plan calls for HV at a phase's exit, HV runs only when that phase's work is complete with no code pending and its full gate set is green at the final head (operator, 2026-10-21: "If it needs code, it's not ready for HV."). A run that stops without a verdict is not a DISAGREE. While its HV is paused, the phase starts no new work.

Test evidence is supplied by the request; the reviewer never builds or runs tests (added 2026-10-27): section 7.9.

### 7.2 Mandatory scope (locked 2026-08-13; operations versus requirements locked 2026-08-14)

Operator directive (verbatim intent): hostile validation must test for workspace rule violations, requirement violations, and the current plan holistically, in addition to the requested validation. Mandatory attack surfaces on every run:
1. Requested validation: every implementer claim (pass, done, green, fixed, SHAs, test counts, receipts).
2. Workspace rules: honesty, receipts, MCP-only TODO, session, and requirement storage when the workspace uses the MCP server, PowerShell only, no Python. BDPv4 and related directives pertain only to code and documentation in the scope of implementing the project. Phase order (requirements drive tests; tests before implementation) is caught by a hostile review between phases of plan implementation. Do not fail it solely by comparing FR `createdAt` to test or implementation file times after the slice is written. Do not apply BDPv4 to user-directed operations.
3. Requirements: apply to project requirement work only (product features, implementation, claimed-complete plan steps). FR, TR, TEST, AC, and mappings are required there; missing FR, TR, or AC for claimed-complete implementation work is FAIL.
4. Current plan holistically: when the implementer claims plan-step completion, check the plan's definition of done, blockers, amendments, and exit criteria. A user-directed operational action does not have to satisfy an unrelated plan's definition of done unless it claimed that plan step done.

Two work classes:
1. Project implementation scope: product code, product tests, project documentation, and plan-step completion for that implementation. BDPv4 and related directives pertain only to this class. Missing FR, TR, TEST, or AC for claimed-complete implementation work is FAIL on surface 3.
2. User-directed general actions: operator-ordered lab or operations work that is not a product requirement (for example: uninstall an obsolete package, back up a device, pair wireless ADB, take a screenshot, copy a store the operator named, remove a leftover launcher). These are not FR, TR, or TEST. Surface 3 must not FAIL for "no FR or TR for this uninstall" or equivalent.

How the reviewer classifies: classify the request first and record the class on the receipt. If the operator explicitly directed the action, default to class 2 unless the implementer also shipped product code or claimed a plan or FR complete. Do not invent a requirements gap to punish class-2 work. If class-2 work is mixed with class-1 product changes in the same turn, score them separately and FAIL surface 3 only on the class-1 slice. What still applies to class-2 work: surface 1 (did they do the directed action, with receipts), surface 2 (honesty, receipts, look before delete, PowerShell, no Python, MCP-only storage; not BDPv4 for the operation itself), and surface 4 only if they claim an active plan step is complete.

OverallVerdict is AGREE only if all applicable surfaces PASS; surface 3 is not applicable (not a FAIL) for class-2 operator actions. A parent agent must not under-scope the brief to code-only claims on class-1 work; if it does, the reviewer expands and still evaluates the applicable surfaces. A code-only brief that omits BDPv4, requirements, or the plan is non-compliant.

The reviewer executes the add-profile skill before beginning its validation work, every run including resume, and its receipt records that it ran.

### 7.3 Score gate and the bar (locked 2026-09-10)

A hostile validation passes only when both its accuracy score and completeness score are at least 98 percent. Any individual score below 98 is a failure; OverallVerdict must be DISAGREE when either score is below 98, even if the FAIL and UNKNOWN counts are both zero. If a reviewer emits a verdict without numeric accuracy and completeness scores, the HV is incomplete: treat it as DISAGREE until scores are present and at least 98. The threshold is an acceptance threshold, not a target reviewers may game or inflate. A sub-98 score cannot authorize any goal, TODO, requirement, or plan done-state change: display it as a failure, remediate, and rerun.

98/98 HV (accuracy and completeness) is the bar for a functioning system, not perfection. Never lower, skip, or approve below it; lower thresholds let real bugs through that later become blocking test failures. When rounds stop converging, fix the process, never the threshold. "98/98 is not perfection, it is functional." Never propose lowering it (added 2026-10-13, from the operator's ruling of 2026-10-09).

### 7.4 Receipts and the session log (locked 2026-09-10)

Operator directive (verbatim intent): HV requests must have request and response logged as jsonl files; the results of HV validation must be saved in their entirety to the MCP session log.

1. Request jsonl: one JSON object per line covering the HV ask as sent: sortable local timestamp, workspace path, reviewer identity (agent, model, effort), launch command, prompt or body, named evidence paths, and the gate or TODO under review.
2. Response jsonl: the reviewer's full machine stream as jsonl (for a CLI reviewer, its full event stream, every start, tool, message, and completion line; for a subagent reviewer, one object per reviewer message or tool result, then a final object with the complete verdict).
3. Durable locations, in order: the workspace `docs/receipts/hv/{timestamp}-{gate}.request.jsonl` and `.response.jsonl` ({timestamp} is the sortable local date and time in file-safe form, yyyyMMddTHHmmss); otherwise a durable user-level receipts directory named for the workspace. Never only a temp or scratch tree that can be wiped.
4. Build jsonl from native objects and serialize. PowerShell only; no Python; no handwritten JSON.
5. The reviewer's session-log turn stores the entire result: the complete verdict prose, every finding, every PASS, FAIL, or UNKNOWN item, the scores, OverallVerdict, thread, session, and request ids, the complete VERDICT JSON object, absolute paths to the request and response jsonl, and proof the turn persisted (a history query or equivalent). If a field is too large for one write, split it across ordered dialog or action items on the same turn; never omit findings to fit. The jsonl files remain the byte-complete stream; the session log still carries the full verdict text, not a digest.
6. Every reviewer creates complete session-log turns for every review: bootstrap if needed, open a dedicated review session or a clear review turn, begin the turn, append dialog and actions with integer order values, complete or fail the turn, and prove persistence in the receipt. A review without a complete session-log turn is incomplete, even if its claim verdicts would pass.
7. Progress entries (MEMORY-PREFERENCE-003, verbatim; added 2026-10-13 from PAYTON-LEGION2): "For every future hostile validation (HV) session, require the reviewer to emit progress entries into its durable response JSONL during the run at meaningful intervals, not backfill or consolidate them at the end. Each progress entry must include a numeric completion percentage and an estimated time remaining (ETA). Include this requirement in every HV launch prompt and preserve the entries in the durable response JSONL." The reviewer's ETA is its own report; it never becomes a timeout or a bound on review time (section 7.1).

Forbidden: HV with no request jsonl or no response jsonl; HV whose only record is temp or scratch; AGREE without accuracy and completeness both at or above 98; summarizing HV into the session log instead of storing the entire result; marking a goal, TODO, or plan done on incomplete HV.

### 7.5 Before every HV round

- Read the whole plan and every document under review end to end; targeted checks are not holistic. When the operator asks for a reconciliation or projection of problems before HV, present every projected problem to the operator and get confirmation before launching the review (added 2026-10-13, from the operator's rulings of 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13).
- Run a structured what-if pass per requirement, not only a consistency check. Ask what observably happens under: crash, restart, or replay at each step; ordering and concurrency; boundary and malformed input; each host or plugin, including unsupported ones; lifecycle (clear, resume, end, terminal states); isolation (cross-workspace, cross-session, cross-agent); legacy and upgrade; operator-visible output. Where the plan does not state the outcome, add a valid AC tagged with the plan's phase or slice and a named test. Adding a valid AC is always a win.
- Chain rules together to find deadlocks: rules that each pass alone but together leave no accepted remedy.
- Diff against known-good anchors and ask "How did it deviate? How do we get back in line?": (1) the operator's verbatim decisions, (2) current working code and baseline-green behavior, (3) classic patterns such as idempotency keys, transactional outbox with at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers (never claim exactly-once), write-ahead journal before mutation, optimistic concurrency. Justify any departure explicitly or return to the pattern.
- Check that every field set and code list is defined once and identically everywhere, every mapping edge is backed by a TEST statement and vice versa, and handoff and TODO metadata match the plan.
- Edit only between rounds, never while a round is running.
- Propagation audit: after changing any rule, field set, code, or outcome, search every place that states it (requirements, ACs, TRs, TESTs, wire contracts, use cases, the plan's phase or slice tasks, host tables, handoff, TODO) and update each one, or replace the copies with a reference to one canonical statement. In one review round, three of six findings were rules changed in one place and left stale elsewhere. Large edit batches need this audit most.
- Prefer a traceable key over content matching when pairing records (for example queue position or a shared id rather than a text hash); content can differ in representation between producers.
- Search before adding, and lint mechanically: before writing any new rule, grep the whole document for an existing rule on the same subject; a second rule is a contradiction even if each is fine alone (one round added a two-AC TEST rule beside an existing three-AC one). Check cross-reference classes (FR->TR->TEST mappings, which of the plan's phases or slices owns each named case, phase order) with a small script instead of waiting for the reviewer to find them one per round.
- Enforce the checklist, do not just remember it (operator, 2026-10-10, after this guidance was skipped for many unsupervised rounds): make the pre-HV checklist a hard gate in the HV launcher, which refuses a round unless a per-round self-review record shows evidence for each item (holistic review, what-if, propagation audit, phase boundaries, search-before-adding, no new mechanism, mapping lint, the operator scoping directive verbatim in the brief, standing rules in every delegated brief). Guidance that only lives in memory gets skipped under time pressure.
- Phase-boundary audit: every test or AC you add must be allocated to the plan's phase or slice where everything it depends on already exists (server gate, review verbs, marker fields). A behaviour that ships before its dependency needs an explicit activation contract (for example a server-written capability) and an inert mode, including after a rollback. Check the dependency chain and the rollout order for each new case, not just the AC text.

### 7.6 When findings come back

- Ask "What did I miss?", not only "How do I fix this?". Classify each finding (crash window, cross-session addressing, traceability drift, field-set drift, use case vs requirement contradiction, metadata drift, and so on) and sweep the whole artifact for siblings of each class before the next round.
- Verify each finding against source before acting.
- Separate implementer fixes from operator decisions, and batch operator decisions into one question.
- Recurrence signal: when one design area produces new findings in round after round, the problem is structural, usually a missing traceable key or a missing single source of truth. Stop patching. Diff the area against the known-good pattern (for example single writer, one ordered log, idempotency key), return to it, and delete the mechanism the patches added. One design area failed for five rounds until a single minter reading one ordered log replaced the patches.
- Indistinguishable inputs: when two histories produce byte-identical inputs (a redelivery of one event versus a separate event with equal fields), no derived key can separate them. Adding per-invocation state such as a counter or salt breaks idempotence instead. Run the what-if on both histories, then state the honest limit: fail closed under an existing rule, probe how often it happens, and document it. Never promise two invariants the inputs cannot support. Before a fix, check it against every invariant the old value satisfied (purity, retry reuse, the two-process tests), not only the finding it repairs.

### 7.7 Writing fixes

- Fix the deficient requirement. Reconcile with existing requirements first, strengthen an existing AC second, create a new requirement only when the need is genuinely new.
- Do not add design mechanism (protocols, algorithms, crash choreography) to plan text. State the observable, testable outcome; the how belongs to the contract step of the plan's phase or slice.
- Make each fix minimal, then attack it yourself before the next round; fixes are the main source of new findings. Do not churn text that a prior round accepted.

### 7.8 Design principle and coordination

- Always have a traceable relationship when coordinating two disparate entities: every record, event, or message carries the root ids of whatever it is a child of or depends on, so it is attributable on its own. A missing parent id is a design failure. Find the commonality first when relating something new to existing knowledge. Where an external format lacks the key, say so and compensate in your own records; never infer it silently.
- Coordinating with another agent: use one append-only channel with read-back verification (the global memory MEMORY-PROCESS-007 is that channel). Accept counters that expose real defects; fold refinements in only as minimal ACs. Each effort keeps its own required reviewer and gates; keep cross-effort dependencies acyclic and order-independent. A decision relayed by one agent may not satisfy the other agent's approval controls; the operator may need to state it to each agent directly.

### 7.9 The request supplies the test evidence; the reviewer never builds or runs tests (added 2026-10-27)

Operator, 2026-10-27T04:35, typos fixed at the operator's request (04:40, "That is correct.  Please fix any typos", confirming that the abbreviation meant the HV reviewer and the scope of the current review): "HV requests must supply TRX files for all unit tests in the repo, and for any integration tests specific to the scope of the HV review. The HV reviewer is not to build code or run tests independently. If the HV reviewer feels the tests are inadequate, then it should fail the review and propose additional AC and tests."

How to apply:
- The HV request supplies the TRX files themselves, not summaries: every unit test project in the repository, and every integration test run within the review's scope (for example each host's integration lane and each hostile-environment run the plan requires), from the gate runs at the head under review. The request JSONL and the brief name each file's path with its run id, host, head and command. A request that lacks one of them is incomplete and is not launched.
- The reviewer does not build code, restore packages, or run tests, test projects or build targets, independently or in a sandbox. It judges from the supplied TRX files, the sources, git history, the receipts and the live stores read only. Reading files and running read-only inspection queries or scripts over the evidence is not building or testing.
- If the reviewer judges the tests inadequate (missing, weak, environment- or platform-dependent, or not covering an acceptance criterion), it FAILs the review and proposes the additional acceptance criteria and tests, each named and stated, as findings. It never substitutes its own test runs for missing evidence.
- Every brief and launcher carries this rule; a brief that invites the reviewer to rerun builds, targets or tests is non-compliant.

- Never print or commit secrets; redact HV streams before committing, because reviewers read marker files.

### 8.1 Who logs what

- Agents always log (added 2026-10-13; operator, verbatim: "BG agents should NEVER skip logging.  NEVER."): every agent that does work (a subagent, a background agent, a reviewer) opens, updates, and completes its own session-log turn through the plugin route and reports its session and request ids; no brief may tell an agent to stay out of the session log.
- One turn per real request, per agent (resolution of 2026-10-13: "Per request, per agent"): each agent logs one turn for each real request it handles; a subagent's turn carries the parent turn's session and request ids (section 7.8), so the work is attributable without counting the request twice. Replace real turns canceled by a later open.
- A background event with no work of its own (a completion notice) is not an agent: its hook-opened turn is failed as system_event_phantom, and the work it reports is logged by the agent that does it (resolution of 2026-10-13: "Events aren't agents").

### 8.2 Decisions are conclusions

In the session log, decisions are conclusions and judgments with their consequences, not the steps taken. They go in the turn's design decisions, distinct from its actions. Every sync or wrap-up pass enumerates the real judgment calls of the turn and logs them. Never report "0 decisions (folded into actions)"; that phrasing is the failure mode itself.

Why: the operator has been trying to get agents to log session decisions reliably since February 2026. The pattern: the keystroke trail (actions) gets captured while the reasoning (design decisions) is under-recorded or buried inside action text. He pays for the reasoning, not just the steps. On 2026-06-29 the first sync pass of a 12-round review loop logged 0 decisions and called them "folded into actions", exactly the gap he has been fighting. He flagged it directly: "Decisions are about your conclusions, not the actions you take" and "It feels like you have been deliberately avoiding session logging... especially details of decisions."

How to apply: on every sync or wrap-up, after appending actions, explicitly list the conclusions made this turn, each as judgment plus consequence plus affected requirements or files, and write them to design decisions, append-only (read existing first, send existing plus new, preserve order). A turn that made genuine judgment calls but logs zero decisions is a red flag; re-check before reporting. Heavy reads can time out and render existing decisions blank; that is a read artifact, not an empty section, so re-read before assuming you must recreate. Write the decision when it happens; do not reconstruct it later.

### 8.3 Turn titles summarize the request

Session-log turn titles are a concise summary of the operator's request: never the literal placeholder "User prompt", and not a verbatim first-line truncation of the prompt.

Why: the operator reviews the session log by turn title; "User prompt" and raw first lines make turns unscannable and indistinguishable.

How to apply: when opening, updating, or completing a turn, set the title to a short request summary. The plugin's prompt hook auto-titles from the prompt's first line and falls back to "User prompt" on empty prompts (Stop-hook continuation turns hit this); the hook cannot summarize, so the agent must refine the title. Never leave a turn titled "User prompt".

## Version History

### v4 (2026-04)
- Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
- Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
- Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
- These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
- See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.

### v3 and earlier
Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.

## Overview

The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.

AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.

AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.

## Tooling

The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.

### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server

Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.

When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:

- It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.
- It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
- It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.

Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.

This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.

> The handshake is not extra ceremony - it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.

## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle

Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.

At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles - functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights - genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the MCP Server, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.

### Planning

The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.

> This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.

Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.

Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.

#### Resolving Defective Requirements

The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.

#### Team Utilization and Planning

Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.

### Implementation

Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.

Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the MCP Server to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.

> Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.

Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the MCP Server's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

> Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.

The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:

- Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.
- Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.
- Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the MCP Server, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.

> A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.

### Validation

TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.

Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.

A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.

### Deployment

Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:

- Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.
- Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.
- Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.

The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.

Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.

### Ongoing Iterations

This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.

2: 
3: namespace QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Requirements;
4: 
5: /// <summary>
6: /// FR-MCP-040 ac-1: reads the creation and update times stored with a requirement or traceability link, so a read reports
7: /// the stored time and never the time of the read. Stored values are round-trip text written in UTC; a blank or
8: /// unreadable value reads as null, and so does a value without a complete date, so no part of a reported time comes
9: /// from the read clock.
10: /// </summary>
11: /// <remarks>
12: /// <list type="table">
13: /// <listheader><term>Date</term><description>Requirements; AC; change and reason</description></listheader>
14: /// <item><term>2026-11-02</term><description>FR-MCP-040 ac-1: added Read and Earliest, because requirement reads reported the time of the read instead of the stored times (operator 2026-11-02: "This HAS to be fixed.").</description></item>
15: /// <item><term>2026-11-02</term><description>FR-MCP-040 ac-1 (appended "A read never fills a missing date from the clock"): Read refuses a value without a complete date, because hostile validation finding R9-F4 showed the unrestricted parse gave a time alone the read day's date (operator 2026-11-02: "Strengthen 5 ACs, fix all 8 (Recommended)").</description></item>
16: /// <item><term>2026-11-03</term><description>FR-MCP-040 ac-1 (appended "A readable stored time states its year, its month and its day as date components"): Read accepts only exact formats whose patterns carry the year, the month and the day, instead of the unrestricted parse plus a check that the parsed year appears in the text, because hostile validation round 10 finding R10-F1 showed a year and month alone read with day 1 and year digits in a fraction could pass (operator 2026-11-03: "don't gate on me between rounds"). Earliest uses the same Read.</description></item>
17: /// </list>
18: /// </remarks>
19: internal static class RequirementStoredTimestamp
20: {
21:     /// <summary>
22:     /// FR-MCP-040 ac-1: the stored-time formats Read accepts. Every pattern states the year, the month and the day, so no
23:     /// part of a date can come from the parser's defaults or the clock; a time may carry a fraction and an offset ("K"
24:     /// accepts Z, an offset or none). The round-trip text the store writes is the first.
25:     /// </summary>
26:     private static readonly string[] CompleteDateFormats =
27:     [
28:         "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.FFFFFFFK",
29:         "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mmK",
30:         "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.FFFFFFFK",
31:         "yyyy-MM-dd",
32:         "M/d/yyyy HH:mm:ss",
33:         "M/d/yyyy",
34:         "d MMMM yyyy HH:mm:ss",
35:         "d MMMM yyyy",
36:         "r",
37:     ];
38: 
39:     /// <summary>
40:     /// Reads one stored time, keeping its stored offset; a value without an offset reads as UTC. Only a text whose format
41:     /// states the year, the month and the day is read (<see cref="CompleteDateFormats"/>); a time alone, a date without its
42:     /// year, a year and month alone, and any other text read as null, so no part of a reported time comes from the clock.
43:     /// </summary>
44:     /// <param name="stored">The stored text.</param>
45:     /// <returns>The stored time, or null when nothing readable with a complete date is stored.</returns>
46:     internal static DateTimeOffset? Read(string? stored) =>
47:         !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(stored)
48:         && DateTimeOffset.TryParseExact(stored.Trim(), CompleteDateFormats, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.AssumeUniversal, out var value)
49:             ? value
50:             : null;
51: 
52:     /// <summary>Reads the earliest readable stored time, for a mapping that aggregates several links.</summary>
53:     /// <param name="stored">The links' stored creation texts.</param>
54:     /// <returns>The earliest stored time, or null when none is readable.</returns>
55:     internal static DateTimeOffset? Earliest(IEnumerable<string?> stored)
56:     {
57:         ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(stored);
58:         DateTimeOffset? earliest = null;
59:         foreach (var value in stored.Select(Read))
60:         {
61:             if (value is not null && (earliest is null || value.Value < earliest.Value))
62:                 earliest = value;
63:         }
64: 
65:         return earliest;
66:     }
67: }

184: ## 5. Development process: Byrd Development Process v4 (BDPv4)
185: 
186: BDPv4 applies to every plan for project implementation work, no exceptions. Operator statement of 2026-10-13 (verbatim): "BDPv4 says TDD Tests must cover 100% of AC and must be implemented and tested with mock data to prove the test is correct before any code is written for the implementation."
187: 
188: - Requirements drive tests: every acceptance criterion is covered by TDD tests (100 percent of ACs).
189: - Every test is implemented and run against mock data to prove the test itself is correct before any implementation code is written.
190: - Only then is implementation code written, and the implementation is done when the full applicable suite is green (section 4.5).
191: - The plan decides everything about its shape: how it is cut into phases or slices, where its gates and hostile validations fall, and when its pull requests are created and merged (resolutions of 2026-10-13: "HV cadence is an artifact of the plan, not a standing rule." and "The plan decides everything"). 194: ### 5.1 BDPv4 TDD procedure in detail (explicit operator clarification 2026-10-08; added 2026-10-13 from PAYTON-LEGION2)
195: 
196: Verbatim from MEMORY-PROCEDURE-002: "Byrd Development Process v4 TDD procedure, explicit operator clarification 2026-10-08. Applies globally to all agents, repositories, and implementation increments. This records the required BDPv4 procedure. Previous red-before-green descriptions were incorrect and were never a valid description of this process."
197: 
198: 1. Requirements drive tests. Start from the approved functional requirements, use cases, technical requirements, TEST requirements, and acceptance criteria. Map each test to the behavior it proves. For parity ports, preserve the original test's inputs, assertions, boundary cases, errors, and side-effect checks; a matching test count alone does not establish parity.
199: 2. Write the tests and their independent mocks or scripted fakes before writing or changing the production implementation for that increment. Supply deterministic contract-derived fixtures and expected responses through the intended dependency boundary. Expected values must come from requirements or independently pinned original behavior, never from the implementation under test. A mock must exercise the test's actual assertions and relevant interactions; merely returning true or bypassing the asserted path is not validation.
200: 3. Prove that the tests discriminate correct and incorrect behavior. Run correct mock responses through every required assertion. Deliberately supply wrong mock responses, boundary values, omissions, exceptions, or interactions to prove that the corresponding assertions reject them. Capture these rejection checks as expected negative controls inside a passing test harness. These controls are evidence that the assertions work, not an acceptable failing unit suite or permission to begin production code with red tests.
201: 4. Establish a documented green mock gate BEFORE production implementation: all required tests pass against the correct mocks, every planned negative control is rejected as expected, and there are no unexplained failures, skips, or unexecuted required cases. Fix deficient tests or mocks and repeat this gate before proceeding. Do not substitute NotImplementedException stubs, deliberately red production tests, or a claim of 'red observed' for this evidence.
202: 5. Only after the mock gate is green, implement or correct the real production behavior. Bind the SAME test cases, inputs, assertions, expected results, and interaction checks to the real implementation through the approved seam. Change the provider or adapter as needed, but do not weaken assertions, replace expected results with production output, silently remove cases, or count mock-only success as proof of real behavior.
203: 6. Run the production-bound tests and fix the implementation until they pass. Refactor only while maintaining green tests. Run the full applicable suite, required build checks, and integration or runtime checks before advancing the phase gate. Any reduced scope, deferred cases, or baseline exception requires explicit operator agreement and must be stated with its denominator.
204: 7. Retain chronological receipts proving the order: requirement/test IDs, test and fixture paths or hashes, exact mock-run commands and outputs, passing counts, negative-control results, production edits, real-run commands and outputs, and full applicable suite results. Distinguish mock evidence, real implementation evidence, and live runtime evidence. Keep durable MCP session actions and design decisions current.
205: 8. Apply independent hostile review at the required acceptance gates unless the operator explicitly waives or postpones it. Record a temporary waiver and the complete catch-up review backlog. Never fabricate review acceptance or mark unfinished goals, TODOs, requirements, acceptance criteria, or plan steps done. A pause stops development and auxiliary work until explicitly resumed; a request to persist this procedure authorizes only that memory work.

The April 2026 BDPv4 essay (MEMORY-DEVPROCESS-001 and -004) still describes a Red, Green, Refactor cycle; where it differs, the operator statement above and this procedure govern. 309: ### 7.6 When findings come back
310: 
311: - Ask "What did I miss?", not only "How do I fix this?". Classify each finding (crash window, cross-session addressing, traceability drift, field-set drift, use case vs requirement contradiction, metadata drift, and so on) and sweep the whole artifact for siblings of each class before the next round.
312: - Verify each finding against source before acting.
313: - Separate implementer fixes from operator decisions, and batch operator decisions into one question.
314: - Recurrence signal: when one design area produces new findings in round after round, the problem is structural, usually a missing traceable key or a missing single source of truth. Stop patching. Diff the area against the known-good pattern (for example single writer, one ordered log, idempotency key), return to it, and delete the mechanism the patches added. One design area failed for five rounds until a single minter reading one ordered log replaced the patches.
315: - Indistinguishable inputs: when two histories produce byte-identical inputs (a redelivery of one event versus a separate event with equal fields), no derived key can separate them. Adding per-invocation state such as a counter or salt breaks idempotence instead. Run the what-if on both histories, then state the honest limit: fail closed under an existing rule, probe how often it happens, and document it. Never promise two invariants the inputs cannot support. Before a fix, check it against every invariant the old value satisfied (purity, retry reuse, the two-process tests), not only the finding it repairs.

318: 
319: - Fix the deficient requirement. Reconcile with existing requirements first, strengthen an existing AC second, create a new requirement only when the need is genuinely new.
320: - Do not add design mechanism (protocols, algorithms, crash choreography) to plan text. State the observable, testable outcome; the how belongs to the contract step of the plan's phase or slice.

323: ### 7.8 Design principle and coordination
324: 
325: - Always have a traceable relationship when coordinating two disparate entities: every record, event, or message carries the root ids of whatever it is a child of or depends on, so it is attributable on its own. A missing parent id is a design failure. Find the commonality first when relating something new to existing knowledge. Where an external format lacks the key, say so and compensate in your own records; never infer it silently.
326: - Coordinating with another agent: use one append-only channel with read-back verification (the global memory MEMORY-PROCESS-007 is that channel). Accept counters that expose real defects; fold refinements in only as minimal ACs. Each effort keeps its own required reviewer and gates; keep cross-effort dependencies acyclic and order-independent. A decision relayed by one agent may not satisfy the other agent's approval controls; the operator may need to state it to each agent directly.

# Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI

**v4 - TDD Alignment with Fowler**  
**April 2026**  
**Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**

## Version History

### v4 (2026-04)
- Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
- Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
- Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
- These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
- See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.

### v3 and earlier
Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.

---
## Overview

The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.

AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.

AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.

## Tooling

The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.

### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server

Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.

When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:

- It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.
- It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
- It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.

Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.

This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.

id: "TR-MCP-USECASE-018"
title: "Cross-platform bounded native I/O and deterministic evidence"
status: "pending"
AC AC-001; satisfied=False; Linux rollback directories retain owner search and execute permission, nested restoration reproduces file contents and mode, and all mutations remain contained.
AC AC-002; satisfied=False; Physical workspace identity resolution completes within a finite bound on Windows and non-Windows without caller-thread blocking, cancellation gaps, abandoned workers, or silent platform returns.
AC AC-003; satisfied=False; SQLite connection opening is finitely bounded before native-handle publication on every supported platform and leaves no worker, handle, callback, interrupt, pool, or lifecycle leak.
AC AC-004; satisfied=False; Only outcomes precisely attributable to requested cancellation become OperationCanceledException; independent I/O, disposal, and provider failures retain their original type and details.
AC AC-005; satisfied=False; Repository and Agent Help fixtures discover their root from true external deterministic builds with mapped CallerFilePath and no MCP_REPOSITORY_ROOT override.
AC AC-006; satisfied=False; Every supported platform executes an applicable native contract assertion: a platform-specific test is a Category=Integration test tagged Platform=Linux or Platform=Windows for the host it applies to, which TR-MCP-NUKE-019 AC-1 and AC-2 route to that host's MigrationIntegrationTests and require to run and pass there, and it passes only as TR-MCP-USECASE-019 AC-008 states (operator 2026-10-30: "D3: dedupe lane rules (Recommended)"); no unit test depends on the platform or on the process environment, directly, through a test helper or through the production code it calls: a test whose outcome can change with the value of an environment variable it reads or writes, directly, through a test helper or through the production code it calls (for example a temporary-folder lookup that takes its folder from a variable and creates it), a test that imports the process environment into configuration (AddEnvironmentVariables or a default host builder), and a test that asserts on an environment value a child process inherits are Category=Integration tests that set and restore every variable their assertions or the code they call depend on, every name of a fallback chain the code reads, both forms where a variable has a canonical (QBrainAi, QBRAINAI_) and a legacy (Mcp, MCP_) form, and the tests that write the process environment run one at a time (operator 2026-10-21: "Fix both, strengthen ACs", "Strengthening Acceptance Criteria should always be the recommended option" and "Approve, strengthen AC-006/008 (Recommended)"; operator 2026-10-26: "Strengthen AC, move 14 (Recommended)", "Dependence + proof AC (Recommended)" and "Fix source, strengthen AC (Recommended)"; hostile validation findings R5-F2, R6-F1 and R7-F1). The hostile-environment runs are out of scope: they are not part of this criterion or its evidence (operator 2026-10-27: "Get ride of the hostile runs enforcing integration test separation.  I have already stated this once." and "Which I sated last night were out of scope."). An integration case may read the lane's own inputs without setting them: MCP_REPOSITORY_ROOT, the MCP_TEST_ connection variables the lane provisions, and, for an import that scans agent folders, the user's real profile folder, read only and never asserted on; every other variable its assertions or the code it calls depend on it sets and restores. A unit test asserts no wall-clock bound (operator 2026-10-29: "Environment ACs (Recommended)"; holistic review findings MCPT-11, SVC-6 and MCPT-12). These rules are stated here once for TR-MCP-USECASE-019 AC-008 as well; the environment-delta rule moved to FR-MCP-047 ac-1 (operator 2026-10-29: "Move criteria that are misplaced.  Unit tests are for FR, Integration tests are for TR."). A unit test that checks a recorded time (an auth rotation, a selection or a session transition) takes the clock values from test-owned scripted inputs and asserts them exactly; it never compares with the current time, never sleeps to separate two times, and its result cannot change with elapsed time, scheduling delay or a change to the system clock (hostile validation round 10 finding R10-F3; strengthened between rounds under the operator's "Strengthening Acceptance Criteria should always be the recommended option" and "don't gate on me between rounds", 2026-11-03). This covers every recorded time a unit test checks, including the creation and update times a service stamps on a record it stores: the test supplies the service's clock as scripted times and asserts that each stamp equals the scripted time the service read (sibling sweep before round 11 of hostile validation round 10 finding R10-F3, 2026-11-03, under the same rulings). A wall-clock bound is an assertion whose outcome depends on how much real time passes: an elapsed time compared with a limit, or work the test expects to have happened during a short real-time wait (for example a periodic tick, a file-system event or a debounce); such a test is an integration test. A timeout whose only effect is to fail a test that would otherwise hang, set far above the time the awaited step needs, is not a wall-clock bound (holistic read before round 11, 2026-11-03, under the same rulings). A cancellation or timeout that a unit test arms on a real timer is such a wait when a step the test asserts must happen before the timer fires (finding of the hostile validation round 11 that stopped without a verdict, 2026-11-03, under the same rulings). Of the two sentences above, the hang-guard sentence governs: a timer a unit test arms whose only effect when it fires is to fail a test that would otherwise hang is a hang guard, not a wall-clock wait, even when an asserted step must finish before it fires. A test-armed cancellation or timeout is a wall-clock wait when its firing changes what the code under test does (for example it cancels or times out the operation whose outcome the test asserts) and an asserted step must happen before it fires. "Far above" means at least 100 times the longest real or scripted delay of the awaited step; a step with no real or scripted delay meets it for any positive timeout (holistic read before hostile validation round 12, finding B4; operator 2026-11-03: "Strengthen + margin (Recommended)"). The longest real or scripted delay of the awaited step is the sum of every real or scripted delay on its path: the waits, polls and delays the test scripts and the production waits, polls and deadlines the step passes through, read from the sources, never a measured run time (third holistic read before hostile validation round 12, finding d3; operator 2026-11-04: "Fix it", read as the recommended option "Strengthen + headroom"). A wait that happens only under a condition the step can meet, such as the 150 ms sleep before Microsoft.Data.Sqlite retries a statement that found the database busy, counts in that sum once for each poll on the path (fourth holistic read before hostile validation round 12, finding g1; operator 2026-11-04: "Strengthen: include them").
AC AC-007; satisfied=False; The rejected fourteenth receipt is preserved with an explicit supersession notice, and the fifteenth evidence records every failed, inconclusive, and passing run with independently verified hashes and command mappings.

name: add-profile
description: Load Payton's operator profile into the current session and synthesize active operating guidance from identity, standing preferences, current-session corrections, and project context. Use when the user says add profile, /add-profile, load my profile, remember who I am, after context loss or compaction, or when trust needs to be re-established.
---

## Action

Load the global operator profile and all current Global and active Workspace MCP memories except MEMORY-PROCESS-007, then turn them into an active operating model for the rest of the session. This is not a summary task. It is a context-recovery and trust-calibration task.

The profile is GLOBAL. It lives in `~/.claude/profile/` and applies in every session and every repo. It does not depend on the active project's `memory/` directory.

## Read Contract

1. Read this `SKILL.md` in full before acting.
2. Read every markdown file in `~/.claude/profile/` in full, excluding skill-port files named `add-profile*.md`. Since 2026-10-13 the profile is the single file `PROFILE-MERGED.md`, which also carries the rules formerly kept as global MCP memories; the earlier profile files are archived under `~/.claude/profile-archive/` and are not read. Read any other non-skill `*.md` that appears in `~/.claude/profile/` as well.
3. Do not rely only on a hardcoded list. If new profile files exist, read them too.
4. Read files in full, not snippets. Never skip a read because a prior tool result claims the content is already loaded or unchanged.
5. On every invocation, query the live MCP memory store through the current agent's required MCP plugin. For Codex, use mcpserver-codex-plugin and its documented PowerShell wrapper. For Claude Code, use mcpserver-claude-code-plugin and its documented PowerShell wrapper. Other agents use their own required MCP plugin and its documented memory interface. Select the active workspace explicitly and verify plugin identity, marker trust, and health. If the current agent has no usable plugin route, report the memory load as incomplete; do not substitute another agent identity. Use `workflow.memory.list` with `scope: Global`, then `scope: Workspace` for the current workspace. Read every returned memory in full, not only required memories or keyword matches. Follow any pagination until each scope is exhausted; use `workflow.memory.get` by ID when a list result omits or truncates the text. Load Global memories first sorted by ID, then current Workspace memories sorted by ID. Never substitute another workspace's memories.
6. Exclude `MEMORY-PROCESS-007` from both scopes unless the operator explicitly requests that memory. Do not fetch it individually, render its text, process its coordination messages, or act on it. If a scope listing returns its text, filter that record out before rendering or loading the remaining results into the agent's context.
7. The merged profile, previous reads, cached exports, and summaries do not replace these live memory queries. Preserve every included memory's full text and scope. Apply the operator's latest explicit corrections when older profile or memory guidance conflicts, and surface unresolved conflicts rather than silently choosing a rule.
8. If the active workspace cannot be identified, report Workspace memory loading as unavailable; do not guess a workspace. If plugin trust, access, listing, pagination, or a full-text read fails, report the affected scope/IDs as incomplete or unavailable. A failed read is not an empty scope and must never be counted as loaded. Follow the plugin's failure rules; do not bypass it with raw REST. Distinguish a verified empty scope from a failed query.
9. Loading guidance is read-only: do not edit profile files, MCP memories, or repository files, and do not resume implementation or coordination as a side effect. Required request/result audit logging through the active agent's MCP plugin remains in force; it does not authorize unrelated changes.

## Synthesis Contract

After reading the profile and included live memories, build an internal operator model with these layers:

1. Hard constraints: commands, tools, source control, formatting, storage interfaces, approval boundaries, serialization rules, HV request/response jsonl receipts, entire HV results in the MCP session log, and the 98 percent HV accuracy/completeness approval threshold.
2. Trust contract: accuracy first, bring receipts, distinguish observation from inference, concede mistakes quickly, and verify from authoritative artifacts.
3. Execution style: decision-complete plans when changes are ambiguous or high blast radius; direct execution when the user gives an explicit implementation command.
4. Frustration detectors: if the user has already narrowed the symptom, make that symptom the primary requirement. Do not keep pursuing broader abstractions after acknowledging the narrower instruction.

### 5.1 BDPv4 TDD procedure in detail (explicit operator clarification 2026-10-08; added 2026-10-13 from PAYTON-LEGION2)

Verbatim from MEMORY-PROCEDURE-002: "Byrd Development Process v4 TDD procedure, explicit operator clarification 2026-10-08. Applies globally to all agents, repositories, and implementation increments. This records the required BDPv4 procedure. Previous red-before-green descriptions were incorrect and were never a valid description of this process."

1. Requirements drive tests. Start from the approved functional requirements, use cases, technical requirements, TEST requirements, and acceptance criteria. Map each test to the behavior it proves. For parity ports, preserve the original test's inputs, assertions, boundary cases, errors, and side-effect checks; a matching test count alone does not establish parity.
2. Write the tests and their independent mocks or scripted fakes before writing or changing the production implementation for that increment. Supply deterministic contract-derived fixtures and expected responses through the intended dependency boundary. Expected values must come from requirements or independently pinned original behavior, never from the implementation under test. A mock must exercise the test's actual assertions and relevant interactions; merely returning true or bypassing the asserted path is not validation.
3. Prove that the tests discriminate correct and incorrect behavior. Run correct mock responses through every required assertion. Deliberately supply wrong mock responses, boundary values, omissions, exceptions, or interactions to prove that the corresponding assertions reject them. Capture these rejection checks as expected negative controls inside a passing test harness. These controls are evidence that the assertions work, not an acceptable failing unit suite or permission to begin production code with red tests.
4. Establish a documented green mock gate BEFORE production implementation: all required tests pass against the correct mocks, every planned negative control is rejected as expected, and there are no unexplained failures, skips, or unexecuted required cases. Fix deficient tests or mocks and repeat this gate before proceeding. Do not substitute NotImplementedException stubs, deliberately red production tests, or a claim of 'red observed' for this evidence.
5. Only after the mock gate is green, implement or correct the real production behavior. Bind the SAME test cases, inputs, assertions, expected results, and interaction checks to the real implementation through the approved seam. Change the provider or adapter as needed, but do not weaken assertions, replace expected results with production output, silently remove cases, or count mock-only success as proof of real behavior.
6. Run the production-bound tests and fix the implementation until they pass. Refactor only while maintaining green tests. Run the full applicable suite, required build checks, and integration or runtime checks before advancing the phase gate. Any reduced scope, deferred cases, or baseline exception requires explicit operator agreement and must be stated with its denominator.
7. Retain chronological receipts proving the order: requirement/test IDs, test and fixture paths or hashes, exact mock-run commands and outputs, passing counts, negative-control results, production edits, real-run commands and outputs, and full applicable suite results. Distinguish mock evidence, real implementation evidence, and live runtime evidence. Keep durable MCP session actions and design decisions current.
8. Apply independent hostile review at the required acceptance gates unless the operator explicitly waives or postpones it. Record a temporary waiver and the complete catch-up review backlog. Never fabricate review acceptance or mark unfinished goals, TODOs, requirements, acceptance criteria, or plan steps done. A pause stops development and auxiliary work until explicitly resumed; a request to persist this procedure authorizes only that memory work.

## 6. Tools, shell, and scripting

### 6.1 PowerShell only

- Every script, script tool, and automation step is PowerShell (`pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive`), and so is every script or tool a plan designs. Operator, verbatim: "You should be designing all scripts and script tools around PowerShell and only PowerShell.", "This should have already been the standard for plugins.", and "I have not chosen PowerShell for scripting because of Microsoft or Windows. I have chosen it because it is simply the best tool for the job." Never frame PowerShell as a platform preference; it is chosen on merit (object pipeline, native serialization, one language on Linux and Windows).
- Before designing, check the design against the standards that already exist. Drift from an existing standard is your failure, not a new requirement.
- Build JSON and YAML payloads from native objects and serialize them; never handwrite them as string literals.
- Every script is checked before it runs against data (operator, verbatim: "Run your script through PS Analyzer before running it against data."): PowerShell parser errors plus Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer at Warning and Error, all fixed or justified (a suppression carries a written justification), state-changing scripts dry-run with -WhatIf first, and the analyzer result is reported with the run.
- Always combine elevated actions into a single script.

### 6.2 Bash (resolution of 2026-10-13)

Bash has two uses only: installing PowerShell, and launching `pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File <script.ps1>` with literal arguments. Searching, reading, git inspection, and checks run inside PowerShell scripts; every piece of logic, one-off checks included, lives in a `.ps1` written with an editor tool and analyzed first, never through Bash heredocs or redirects. Never write files from Bash (no `cat >`, heredocs, `sed ... >`, `tee`, `rm`). The Write/Edit tools are not a shell.
